To give your opinion: creo que, pienso que, en mi opinión, para mí.
To agree or disagree politely: (no) estoy de acuerdo, tienes razón, depende.
To link ideas with connectors: además, sin embargo, aunque, en cambio, así que.
To present advantages and disadvantages: por un lado… por otro…
To discuss the environment and city life.
The city council wants to ban cars in the city centre. Over dinner, the friends have different opinions.
In my opinion, it’s a fantastic idea. The centre is very polluted.
I agree with you. Besides, there will be less noise and more space for walking.
On the one hand, you’re right. But on the other, I’m thinking about older people. How will they get to the doctor?
That’s true. My grandmother can’t walk far, and the metro has lots of stairs.
Yes, but there are electric buses. And taxis will be allowed in.
I think the problem is something else: public transport is very expensive.
I disagree. In Madrid it’s quite cheap. London, on the other hand…
Don’t talk to me about London! A metro ticket there costs six pounds.
I think it depends. Although the idea is good, it has to be done gradually.
First, more bike lanes. Then, car parks outside the centre. And finally, the car ban.
Totally agree. So… a toast to the future mayor of Madrid!
“por un lado” = on the one hand
“no me hables” = don’t talk to me
Make a small pause after a connector, like a comma: “Además, …”, “Sin embargo, …”. It makes your argument clearer.
Contaminación, opinión, situación: stressed on the last syllable.

Careful: “No creo que…” (I don’t think that) needs a special mood in Spanish, the subjunctive (No creo que SEA verdad), which you learn at B1. For now use the positive form: “Creo que no es verdad” (I think it isn’t true). It’s perfectly correct!
You say “estoy de acuerdo”, with ESTAR, not “soy de acuerdo”. And “with you” = “contigo” (not “con ti”). Similarly: conmigo (with me).
Connectors turn separate sentences into a real argument. Here are the most important ones:
but, however, on the other hand
así que, por eso, por lo tanto
A car is comfortable; however, it pollutes a lot.
Although it’s expensive, it’s worth it.
“Como” at the start of a sentence means “as / since”: “Como llovía, no salimos” = As it was raining, we didn’t go out.
On the one hand… On the other hand…
The structure of a good argument: your opinion → 2 arguments (además) → a counter-argument (sin embargo) → conclusion (así que / en conclusión).
reciclar el plástico / el vidrio / el papel
ir en bici / a pie / en transporte público
to go by bike / on foot / by public transport
“I think it isn’t true.” (the A2 form)
In my opinion, we need to recycle more.
Although the idea is good, it has to be done gradually.
Lena tried living without plastic for a month. Here are her conclusions, in a blog post.
A month ago I decided to live without plastic for thirty days. Was it easy? Not at all.
On the one hand, I discovered that it’s possible to change lots of habits.
I buy my fruit at the market, with my own cloth bags. Besides, it’s cheaper than in the supermarket.
I always carry a metal bottle, so I don’t buy water any more.
On the other hand, some things are very hard. Almost all cleaning products come in plastic.
Although I looked for alternatives, I didn’t find a single bulk shop in my neighbourhood.
Tom, on the other hand, thinks my experiment is pointless: “One person can’t change anything.”
I disagree with him. I think small changes matter, because they inspire other people.
In fact, Ana and Mihai have already started carrying their own bags.
In conclusion: living without plastic is almost impossible; however, living with much less plastic is very easy.
And you, what do you think? Would you give it a try?

Leo, Pablo’s son, is ten. This week at school he has to prepare a debate on a very important topic: “Should phones be banned at school?”.
The teacher split the class into two groups. Leo had to argue that yes, they should be banned. The problem: he didn’t agree.
“But I love my phone!”, he told his father at home. “How can I argue for something I don’t believe?”
Pablo smiled. “That’s exactly why it’s a good exercise. Let’s look for arguments together.”
At dinner, the whole family helped. Grandma Rosario said: “In my opinion, children today don’t talk to each other at break any more. They just look at a screen.”
Elena, his mother, added: “Besides, studies say phones reduce concentration.”
And his six-year-old sister Nora said very seriously: “And without a phone you play more football.” Everyone laughed.
Leo wrote all the arguments on a sheet of paper. But he also thought about the counter-arguments, because he knew the other group would use them.
On the one hand, a phone is useful for calling your parents in an emergency. On the other hand, the school has a phone for that.
On the day of the debate Leo was nervous. The other group spoke first: “Phones are useful for looking up information and learning.”
When it was his turn, he stood up and said: “I agree that phones are useful. However, at school we have computers for that.”
“Besides, although we love our phones, we all know we don’t talk at break any more. So I think it’s better to leave them at home, at least for a few hours a day.”
His group won the debate. The teacher congratulated him: “You defended an opinion that wasn’t yours very well. That’s very hard.”
That evening Pablo asked him: “So what do you really think now?”.
Leo thought for a moment. “I think my group was right,” he said. “But don’t tell my friends.”
The next day Leo went to school and left his phone in his backpack all day. At break he played football with his friends. He scored two goals.
